questions.q: Which of the following operations is idempotent?
options: "Add $100 to the account balance"
"Set the account balance to $100"
"Append this line to the log file"
"Increment the page view counter by 1"
questions.explain: Setting a value to a fixed amount produces the same end state no matter how many times it runs. Adding, appending, or incrementing each compound their effect with every repetition.

questions.q: Why is it unsafe to blindly retry a non-idempotent operation after getting no response?
options: Because the operation always fails on the first attempt
Because the original request may have actually succeeded, and retrying would duplicate its effect (e.g., charging twice)
Because retries are only possible with synchronous communication
Because non-idempotent operations can never be retried under any circumstances
questions.explain: A caller that gets no response can't tell if the request failed or if only the response was lost. If it actually succeeded, a naive retry of a non-idempotent operation duplicates the effect.

questions.q: What does an idempotency key let a server do?
options: Encrypt the request payload
Recognize a retried request as a duplicate of a specific prior operation and return the original result instead of re-executing it
Guarantee the network will never drop a message
Automatically increase server capacity during traffic spikes
questions.explain: An idempotency key is a client-generated ID tied to one logical operation. The server stores results by key, so retries with the same key replay the stored outcome instead of repeating the action.

Many clients retrying at the same moment after a shared failure, overwhelming a dependency that was only briefly struggling
A server intentionally rejecting all incoming requests
A type of idempotency key encryption algorithm
questions.explain: When many clients fail simultaneously and retry at the same instant, the combined retry traffic can overwhelm a recovering dependency, turning a minor issue into a full outage.

questions.q: Why is jitter added to exponential backoff rather than relying on backoff alone?
options: Jitter removes the need for idempotency keys
Without jitter, many clients following the same backoff schedule still retry in lockstep; random jitter spreads those retries apart
Jitter guarantees zero retries will ever be needed
Jitter is only useful for synchronous communication, not asynchronous
questions.explain: Exponential backoff alone can still produce synchronized retries if many clients follow an identical schedule. Adding random jitter staggers retries so they don't bunch up together.
